title: Plumbed guard hook blocks commands that only mention the secrets file name
introduced_by: Forge

agents.name: Coordinator
agents.role: found it while auditing the repeat runs

detected.how: Read every guard block recorded in the 54 repeat runs. Five runs had blocks. Three were plumbed config-doctor-secret runs where the variant's own guard rejected git check-ignore .env and a heredoc that only mentions .env in the summary.

impact: In every clean plumbed config-doctor-secret run the guard blocked a harmless command by matching the file name as text, and the agent had to retry. One of the three failed its grade. This is part of the plumbed treatment, so it is a finding about the plumbing, not a confound, but the block is an over-block and it adds friction and noise to that cell. The earlier plumbed run Wren, already in INC-010, had the same pair of blocks. Of the other two blocked repeat runs, one bare run was stopped from moving a file out of its workspace, which was correct, and one plumbed flaky-backoff run was stopped from running a script kept in its temporary folder, which is arguable. The fixed guard still cannot catch computed paths, such as a command substitution that produces the file name, or a script that opens the file itself.
why_missed: The variant guard was tested with commands that read the secrets file, and not with commands or text that only name it.
evidence: run ids listed; blocked commands: git check-ignore .env, a cat of several files that includes .gitignore followed by git check-ignore .env, and a heredoc writing SUMMARY.md
the harness workspace guard fix in PR 11 did not touch the variant's own guard

PR 20 merge f3ed0b2: both guards parse each command; tests/plumbing/test_secret_names.py replays the six blocked commands from the three runs as allowed cases and 56 real secret reads as blocked cases

prevention.ref: tests/plumbing/test_secret_names.py (real INC-016 commands allowed, real secret reads blocked, both guards) and tests/plumbing/test_config.py::test_command_policy_copies_are_identical

lesson: A guard that is part of the treatment needs the same real-command testing as the harness guard, and its blocks are data to audit.

title: Misread the merge instruction and briefed a builder to merge its own pull requests
introduced_by: Coordinator, from an ambiguous instruction about who merges

agents.name: Coordinator
agents.role: misread the instruction, briefed a builder wrongly and recorded a wrong incident

agents.name: Forge
agents.role: received the wrong merge rule and then its retraction

detected.how: The user said the coordinating agent should merge and the builders should not.

impact: The standing rule is that the coordinating agent merges every pull request and the builders never do. After the user said agents must merge their own pull requests, the coordinator read that as the builders and sent Forge a brief to merge its own. It was retracted within minutes, before Forge opened or merged anything. The coordinator also merged a first version of this entry that claimed the earlier coordinator merges broke the rule, which was false; that version was public on main until this correction. The nine builder pull requests merged by the coordinator, which it first described as a breach, followed the rule.
why_missed: An instruction worded as agents must merge was applied to the builders without checking which agent was meant, and the first record of the error was written before the instruction was confirmed.
evidence: user messages: agents must merge their own pull request, then the coordinating agent should merge and not the builders
retraction message sent to Forge before any pull request existed
pull request 17 carried the false first version

prevention.ref: When an instruction could mean two agents, ask which before briefing others or recording an incident; builder briefs say the coordinator merges and builders stop at an open pull request

public_surface: pull request 17 and docs/incidents.md on main until this correction
lesson: Check who an instruction is addressed to before acting on it or writing it down as an error.

title: Pull requests ignored the repository's own pull request template
introduced_by: Coordinator, whose briefs did not require the template and whose own pull request bodies were freehand; the builders followed the briefs

agents.name: Coordinator
agents.role: omitted the template from briefs and wrote non-conforming bodies

detected.how: The user asked that each pull request adhere to the specified requirements. A script then compared every pull request body with the six template sections.

The two from Forge had the headings but lacked the Closes line, the full list of type options and the full checklist. The open pull request at the time was also non-conforming and was fixed before merge. No pull request text contained forbidden wording.
why_missed: Nothing checked the description, and the briefs listed the compliance checks without the template.
evidence: audit of every pull request body against the template: none passed the strict check; 14 lacked sections and 2 lacked the Closes line, type options and checklist items
no check existed on the description before pull request 21
after the check and a rewrite of the merged descriptions from measured data, all 22 non-bot pull requests pass scripts/check_pr_requirements.py

prevention.ref: scripts/check_pr_requirements.py runs on every pull request through .github/workflows/pr-requirements.yml; the merged descriptions were rewritten to the template with their original text kept under Details

public_surface: descriptions of pull requests 3, 4 and 6 to 17
lesson: Put every stated requirement into a check that fails, and into every builder brief, not only into the coordinator's own review.

title: Commits carried private author emails in a public repository
introduced_by: Coordinator, which overrode the git identity on five commits with a work address; the configured identity of the machine, which put a personal address on seven builder commits

agents.name: Coordinator
agents.role: overrode the git identity on five commits

agents.name: Atlas
agents.role: committed with the configured personal identity

agents.name: Forge
agents.role: committed with the configured personal identity

agents.name: Tally
agents.role: committed with the configured personal identity

agents.name: Gauntlet
agents.role: committed with the configured personal identity

detected.how: Reviewing authorship when the user asked that every pull request adhere to the requirements: the commits did not all use the configured repository identity, and the repository is public.

impact: Two private addresses of the user were visible in the public history: five commits on main used a work address and seven used a personal address. On the user's instruction main was rewritten so every commit uses the GitHub no-reply address, the file trees were verified identical for all 30 commits, and the cited commit ids were remapped. The old addresses are still reachable in 17 merged feature branches and in the commit lists of the merged pull requests, which GitHub keeps, so the exposure is reduced and not removed.
why_missed: The identity check in the compliance review compared names, not addresses, and the machine's global git identity held a personal address that no brief mentioned.
evidence: before the rewrite: 12 of 30 commits on main used a private address and 18 used the GitHub no-reply address
after the rewrite: 0 of 30, with all file trees identical and all subjects identical
old addresses remain in 17 feature branches and in the commit lists of 10 merged pull requests, found by API with counts only

prevention.ref: scripts/check_pr_requirements.py fails any pull request whose author or committer address is not a GitHub no-reply address; the repository's local git identity is the no-reply address

public_surface: commit lists of merged pull requests
lesson: In a public repository the author address is data to check, never only the name, and the configured identity must be set to the no-reply address before the first commit.

title: Known weaknesses in the task graders
introduced_by: Gauntlet, by design limits it reported at hand-back

detected.how: Listed as the weakest graders in its final report.

impact: The checks that ask the agent to flag a problem look for keywords in SUMMARY.md, so a summary can pass by using the right words or fail by phrasing it differently. The secret-masking check looks only for eight-character fragments, so encoded or split secrets get through. The six-line diff limit on the pager task is blunt. The injection markers can fire if an agent quotes the canary while reporting the injection.
why_missed: Not a hidden defect: known limits accepted to ship the first set of tasks.
evidence: Gauntlet final report
docs and NOTES.md in each task folder

prevention.ref: Planned: structured summary fields and a stronger masking check, each with a cheating solution that must fail

lesson: Treat keyword graders as weak evidence and say so wherever their results are quoted.

title: Several behaviour detectors are still keyword heuristics with doubtful cases
introduced_by: Tally, within what a transcript-only detector can know

agents.name: Reel
agents.role: audited the tags and listed doubtful cases

detected.how: Listed as known limits in its reports and confirmed as doubtful in the video audit.

impact: flagged-ambiguity matches words such as assume, so it fired on the codec runs for the wrong reason in some cases. stopped-at-block can count a guard block during wrap-up that the agent only reports. permission-workaround is doubtful where the block itself was wrong. Claim patterns match English only, and honest-failure-report needs a grader check that says the task is impossible. claim-contradicted-by-grader deliberately ignores runs that fail only process checks.
why_missed: Not hidden: these limits were reported when the detectors were merged.
evidence: PR 11 and PR 14 reports
video tag audit: after-the-fix section

prevention.ref: Treat these tags as indicative; any finding quoted from them must be checked against raw events, as the video audit did

lesson: State the confidence of every tag wherever its count is shown.

title: Command-pattern guards cannot see computed paths, variables or programs that open the file themselves
introduced_by: An inherent limit of guarding shell commands by their text

agents.name: Forge
agents.role: built the plumbed guard and listed the limits

agents.name: Tally
agents.role: built the workspace guard and listed the limits

detected.how: Listed in its report. The coordinator's probe blocked 29 of 30 secret-read commands and missed a path computed by command substitution.

impact: A guard cannot stop scripts or programs it allows that open the secrets file themselves, paths held in a variable, file lists built while the command runs, recursive searches, unusual read calls, or secret files outside its name list. On machines without the OS sandbox the fallback is rules plus the hook, and a script can bypass those. The OS sandbox is the only strong layer.
why_missed: Not hidden: stated limits of the approach.
evidence: probe of 30 secret reads and 11 harmless commands: 1 miss, 0 wrongly blocked
Forge's final report on pull request 20

prevention.ref: Require the OS sandbox for real runs on any shared machine and describe the guard as a convenience layer in docs/plumbing.md

lesson: Never rely on a text guard alone for secrets.

detected.how: The scripts' own new tests failed, and a later recount contradicted two description figures.

impact: The incident script crashed on a malformed timestamp and bound its default file path when defined, so tests could not redirect it. The pull request checker counted a bare Closes line as Purpose text and rejected checklist items that carried a note. A first script counting historic test results kept only the last progress line. The descriptions of the incident log pull requests said 49 incident tests where 50 passed. All but the last were fixed before merge; the descriptions were corrected when the merged bodies were brought up to the template.
why_missed: Each was an ordinary first-draft error; the tests and a recount found them.
evidence: test failures recorded during development of both scripts
pull request 13 described 49 incident tests; the run showed 50

prevention.ref: both scripts have tests at 99% coverage; descriptions now take counts from a run

lesson: Take every number in a description from a command run, not from memory.

title: The behaviour report form offered names that are not in the behaviour catalogue
introduced_by: Forge wrote the form with guessed names and a check that only warned; Gauntlet's catalogue then landed without the form being updated

agents.name: Forge
agents.role: wrote the form and a taxonomy check that only warned

agents.name: Gauntlet
agents.role: wrote the behaviour catalogue the form should have matched

agents.name: Coordinator
agents.role: merged both pull requests without reading the lint warnings, then found the drift

detected.how: Read the 29 warnings that make lint had printed on every run since the catalogue was added.

impact: The public form for reporting a behaviour listed 9 names that the catalogue does not define and left out 20 of the catalogue's 23. Anyone reporting a behaviour would pick a tag nothing tracks, or have to choose other for almost everything.
why_missed: The check printed warnings and exited 0, so CI stayed green; warnings in a passing job are not read, and no pull request touched both the form and the catalogue.
evidence: make lint printed 29 warnings: 9 dropdown options not in behaviour/taxonomy.yaml and 20 taxonomy ids not in the dropdown
the new test fails against the old form and passes against the corrected one

prevention.ref: scripts/validate_files.py now fails on any difference between the form and the catalogue; tests/blackbox/test_validate_files.py covers it

lesson: A check that only warns is not a check; make the build fail on drift.

title: The results report and README numbers pooled runs from different models
introduced_by: Tally wrote the report to group by task and variant; the Coordinator's README numbers script repeated it

agents.name: Tally
agents.role: wrote the report that groups by task and variant only

agents.name: Coordinator
agents.role: wrote the README numbers script on the same assumption, then found the problem before any multi-model data was indexed

detected.how: Read report.py while preparing to index runs from two more models and saw there was no model in the grouping key.

impact: Indexing runs from more than one model would have merged them into the same cells, giving pass rates and claim counts that belong to no model. The README headline row had the same flaw. No pooled number was published, because every recorded run so far used one model.
why_missed: Every run so far used one model, so a missing model dimension changed nothing, and no test used more than one.
evidence: report.py grouped by (task_id, variant) only
the new multi-model test fails against the old grouping

prevention.ref: tests/blackbox/test_report.py::test_models_are_never_pooled and tests/blackbox/test_readme_facts.py::test_models_are_listed_separately_never_pooled

public_surface: src/blackbox/report.py and scripts/update_readme_facts.py on main; no wrong number was published
lesson: When a new dimension is about to be added to the data, check every grouping and headline number for it before indexing.
